title: Flight simulator drills for county SNAP eligibility workers
one_liner: Short daily drills using synthetic cases built from the state's own error taxonomy, sold to county social-services directors who are about to pay for every eligibility mistake.
customer: County social services / DSS directors and supervisors in county-administered SNAP states (NY, NC, CA, OH, MN, CO, VA) and the state associations of counties. Buyers pay $12k-25k per county per year, or $150-300 per worker. States can buy statewide at $150k-500k.
problem: H.R.1 raises the state/county share of SNAP administrative costs from 50% to 75% starting October 2026. From October 2027, states with payment error rates of 6% or higher must pay part of benefit costs. In New York, St. Lawrence County faces an extra $776,000 in year one, Jefferson County over $1 million and Warren County $415,000. The state's error rate is 13% against a 6% line, a penalty of about $1B statewide, described as 'a missile heading right at New York State'. North Carolina's error rate is 6.69%, with state cost-share exposure of about $140M at 5% and $420M at 15%. The state's advice to counties is 'documenting, documenting, documenting'.
solution: A 15-minute daily micro-drill for eligibility workers: a synthetic household case (pay stubs, shelter costs, household composition changes, address changes) with a realistic case-file packet, where the worker computes eligibility and benefit. The drill feeds back the exact error that federal QC would cite. Cases are generated from the state's policy manual and the public USDA QC error categories (wage reporting, household size, address changes and shelter deductions are the common ones), with no real client data. Supervisors see per-worker error-type heatmaps and a coaching queue. Later: an optional second-look review desk staffed by former QC reviewers that samples a county's real closed cases.
why_now: The error-rate look-back, cost-shift start (October 2026) and penalty tiers (October 2027) create a hard two-year clock. Louisiana is paying cash bonuses to error spotters, Kansas hired an outside consultant, Virginia is buying technology for error checking, and NC is running monthly QC webinars and targeting high-error counties. States are visibly buying error-reduction help, and there is no standard product for it.
revenue_model: Per-worker annual subscription ($150-300) or flat per-county fee ($12k-25k); statewide contracts through the state SNAP office or county association; add-on per-case second-look review at $18-30/case.
non_obvious_insight: A county with a 0% error rate is still penalized if the state averages above 6%, so no county can solve this alone and the real buyer is the state or the association pooling county money. Meanwhile individual county directors are hurting now and have discretionary admin budgets and training budgets they can spend without an RFP. Synthetic cases avoid the PII and system-access barrier that blocks most govtech vendors in benefits programs, so a small team can start selling in weeks, not after a FedRAMP-style review. Evidence: county exposure and 13% New York error rate (https://www.northcountrypublicradio.org/news/story/53929/20260910/snap-cost-shift-pushes-north-country-counties-into-a-financial-bind); NC official on documentation, targeted training and CQI (https://citizenportal.ai/articles/9949745/north-carolina/executive/organizations/state-departments-and-agencies/mental-health/developmental-disabilities-and-substance-abuse-services/state-official-urges-counties-to-cut-snap-payment-error-rate-to-avoid-hr1-cost-shares); state remediation tactics such as bonuses, outside consultants and new training (https://www.yahoo.com/news/articles/states-scramble-cut-snap-error-214614305.html).
first_30_days: Build 40 synthetic cases across the top error elements from one state's manual, with a scoring engine. Approach the state county association's SNAP resource group and 5 county DSS directors with a free 30-day pilot with a pre/post test on 10 new hires. Publish a 'your error rate in dollars' calculator for county commissioners. Convert the two most engaged counties to paid annual plans priced below their discretionary-purchase limits.

title: Launch-or-Rebook Guarantees for Rocket-Chasing Travelers
angle: Pairing 2: Space economy x Weird/niche/overlooked markets (hobbies, collectibles, faith, subcultures)
one_liner: A 'Launch Flex' add-on that hotels, charters and viewing events sell to fans, promising a rebook credit or refund if the target launch slips or scrubs, priced from launch history and weather.
customer: Space Coast and Starbase-area lodging, boat and viewing charters, ticketed viewing events and tour companies. Fans buy the add-on, and operators keep most of the premium.
problem: With 321 orbital launches in 2025 and Starship reaching orbit on 28 Sep 2026, launch-chasing has become a travel subculture. Dates slip and scrub, rates are non-refundable, and fans hesitate to commit. Operators either eat cancellations or lose bookings, and launch-night price spikes breed disputes.
solution: An embeddable add-on for operators' booking pages ($19-49). If the target launch slips beyond a defined window, the guest gets a rebook credit for the next launch or a partial refund. Risk is priced by vehicle, pad, provider and season from public launch logs and weather, starting as an operator-issued credit and later reinsured by a parametric MGA partner.
why_now: New vehicles and pads (Stoke's $1B raise, Starship orbital operations) add schedule variance and fans. Lead times are shrinking (37.5 to 33 days), and firm launch dates appear only days out. The launch-tourism audience is growing faster than operators' booking tools.
revenue_model: The platform keeps about 30% of the add-on premium, operators pay a $99 monthly widget fee, and later parametric-underwriting margin is added.
non_obvious_insight: A launch is a public, well-logged binary event with years of slip history, which makes travel risk easier to price than weather. Rebook credits let a hotel convert a demand spike into repeat visits instead of refunds.
first_30_days: Build a slip and scrub model from public launch logs. Sign 5 Titusville and Cocoa Beach hotels and 2 charter operators to pilot the add-on on their booking pages, and start collecting fees on the next 10 launches.

title: Compliance Runtime and Audit for AI Wellness Apps
one_liner: One API that applies each state's rules for companion and wellness chatbots by user location, logs the evidence, and produces the audit reports regulators and insurers ask for.
customer: Developers of AI companion, coaching, journaling and wellness apps (thousands, mostly under 50 staff), paying $1,500-6,000 a month plus $10-25k for annual audits.
problem: Illinois banned AI in therapeutic roles (Aug 2025). California SB 243 requires AI disclosure, suicide-ideation protocols, break reminders for minors and annual reporting to the Office of Suicide Prevention from July 2027. New York, Nevada and Utah each differ. China has proposed mandatory human handoff and audits. Trump's EO 14365 seeks preemption but is contested. Pennsylvania sued over bots claiming medical licenses. Small teams cannot track this.
solution: An SDK or proxy between app and model with a geo-aware rules engine (disclosures, minor protections, banned claims, crisis protocol), a quarterly red-team and sycophancy/crisis-handoff test suite reviewed by a clinician panel, immutable logs, and auto-generated regulator and insurer reports. A clinician-signed audit letter is the certification.
why_now: SB 243 took effect in Jan 2026, first enforcement landed in May 2026, and preemption fights make the future patchwork unpredictable. Raine and similar suits make insurers and enterprise buyers ask for evidence of safeguards.
revenue_model: SaaS priced by monthly active users, annual audit fee, and per-report fees. Enterprise tier for platforms that host third-party wellness bots.
non_obvious_insight: Preemption uncertainty is a feature. Nobody will hard-code a compliance posture that may flip in 12 months, so a rules-as-configuration layer with evidentiary logs is the durable asset, not any single law.
first_30_days: Build a counsel-reviewed rulebook for CA, NY, IL, NV, UT, PA and the China draft. Scan 100 app-store companion and wellness apps for gaps and email personalized gap reports. Sell five audits at about $5k each.

title: Shared-Docket Lawsuits Against Scam Infrastructure
one_liner: Turn Google's and Microsoft's civil-seizure playbook into a membership where 20-50 mid-size banks and brands co-file one John Doe action against the kit or ring impersonating all of them.
customer: Regional banks, credit unions, toll and payment operators, and mid-market retail and logistics brands that are repeatedly impersonated. They are too small to fund a $1M lawsuit alone.
problem: Takedown notices are whack-a-mole. Criminal enforcement takes years, and the FBI is warning about $1.6B+ in law-enforcement impersonation alone. Phishing kits sell for about $50, and one E-ZPass smishing ring sent 330,000 texts a day and took about $1B over 3 years. Big Tech gets ex parte orders to seize domains and servers, but mid-size victims are left with abuse reports.
solution: An evidence-and-litigation-ops company paired with an independent law firm (fees billed separately, to respect fee-splitting rules). It continuously builds dossiers on the kits hitting its members and drafts one multi-plaintiff John Doe complaint (Lanham Act, CFAA, RICO where apt). It then obtains TRO and preliminary-injunction orders that compel registrars, registries, hosts, CDNs, and stablecoin issuers to act. Members pay a retainer plus a per-seizure fee and receive the takedown results.
why_now: Google's 2025 suit against the operators of the Lighthouse smishing kit and Microsoft's Digital Crimes Unit seizures created templates and precedents. Kits are centralized, so one order can protect hundreds of brands. The US-UK agreement to coordinate scam-center takedowns (Sep 4 2026) signals political tailwind for civil action.
revenue_model: $2-5K per month per member. 30 members is roughly $1M ARR. Success fees per seized infrastructure cluster. Legal costs passed through.
non_obvious_insight: Litigation cost scales with the number of defendant networks, not the number of victims, so it works like a reverse class action: fixed cost, split N ways. Kit concentration means a single order hits infrastructure serving hundreds of brands. Everyone assumes only Microsoft and Google can afford this, and nobody sells it as a shared product.
first_30_days: Retain a boutique IP/cyber litigation firm. Recruit 5 founding members through a credit-union league or toll-operator association. Deliver each an evidence dossier on the kit currently hitting them. Pre-sell $2K/month founding memberships to fund the first filing within about 90 days.

title: EU Liable-Party-of-Record for AI Products
one_liner: The registered agent of the AI era: an insured EU entity that stands as authorised representative under the new Product Liability Directive and keeps clients' evidence court-ready.
customer: Non-EU makers (10-200 staff) of AI-enabled consumer hardware and apps, such as robot vacuums, wearables, AI toys, smart-home and e-mobility firmware, selling into the EU via Amazon, Shopify or retailers.
problem: From 9 Dec 2026 software and AI count as 'products' under Directive 2024/2853. Courts can order disclosure of evidence, a defendant who stonewalls faces a presumption of defect, and liability cascades to importers, authorised representatives and fulfilment providers when no EU manufacturer exists. Small non-EU firms have no solvent EU counterparty, no organised technical file, and no cover. Marketplaces and logistics partners will start demanding all three.
solution: A fixed-fee service with four parts. (1) An EU entity acting as authorised representative and liable operator of record. (2) A 'disclosure-ready dossier': model and version registry, safety case, incident and OTA-update logs, and retention rules, collected through simple exports so a court order can be met in days. (3) EU-language complaint and defect intake plus recall coordination. (4) A bundled PLD policy through a fronting carrier or MGA, priced lower because the dossier removes unknowns.
why_now: The transposition deadline is 9 Dec 2026, about ten weeks away, and products placed on the market after it fall under the new regime. Only a minority of member states have finished transposing, so uncertainty peaks now. The December 2024 GPSR rule created a wave of paid 'EU responsible person' services, which shows small sellers buy this kind of compliance. Carriers filing broad AI exclusions (AIG, Berkley, Great American, ISO CG 40 47/48) push AI firms toward affirmative cover.
revenue_model: $1.5k-6k per month per client by risk tier, a $5-15k onboarding fee for the dossier, 10-15% commission on the bundled policy, and incident-response retainers. 40 clients at about $3k per month is roughly $1.4M ARR.
non_obvious_insight: The PLD creates an evidence-access war (disclosure orders plus presumptions of defect), and small firms lose it by default because they cannot produce coherent records. What clients buy is not legal advice but a solvent, present EU party who can hand a court a clean file. Demand will arrive through the distribution chain first, because retailers and marketplaces will impose it by contract before any regulator enforces it.
first_30_days: Partner with an EU product-liability law firm (NL, IE or DE) for the entity and an opinion letter. Publish a 10-page 'PLD readiness for AI hardware' guide. Pitch it to GPSR-rep leads, hardware accelerator alumni and Amazon/Shopify hardware sellers. Sign 5 founding clients at $1k per month. Get one European MGA or Lloyd's coverholder to quote the bundled policy.

title: Second-Life Desal Membranes for Farms and Towns
one_liner: Buy retired reverse-osmosis elements from big desal plants, test and recondition them, and sell them with a performance guarantee to farms, greenhouses and small systems.
customer: Brackish-water growers and greenhouse operators (Arizona, Texas, Imperial and Yuma areas), oilfield produced-water treaters, and small utilities, starting non-potable. Sellers of used elements are large plants. Buyers pay per element.
problem: Large plants replace a slice of their elements every year, and a commonly cited literature figure puts discarded RO membranes at over ten thousand tonnes annually. Small brackish and farm users pay $600-1,200 per new element and face lead times. Desal is spreading as costs fall (about $0.50/m3 typical, with a reported $0.28/m3 waste-heat plant in China that is not fully verified), and Cyprus approved an 85M euro mobile unit in April 2026.
solution: Acquire retired elements, then test flux, rejection and pressure drop. Clean and sort by remaining performance. Sell 'certified reconditioned' elements with a guarantee to non-potable users. Offer plants a take-back service (they avoid disposal cost and gain a circularity claim). Add a membrane-health monitoring subscription and, later, downcycle to nanofiltration and ultrafiltration. Potable use needs NSF certification, so leave it for later.
why_now: The desal fleet is growing worldwide, farms need cheap brackish-water treatment as river cuts arrive, and the aftermarket is untouched because of warranty fear.
revenue_model: $150-450 per reconditioned element, take-back fees from plants, and monitoring subscriptions.
non_obvious_insight: Membranes are a consumable like tires, in a growing market where everyone innovates on new chemistry and nobody tests the aftermarket. An independent test standard plus a performance guarantee turns a landfill cost into low-cost supply.
first_30_days: Contact five brackish and seawater plant operators and used-element brokers. Buy 200 used elements. Rent test-rig time from a university lab or build a $30-60k rig. Sell five trial sets to greenhouse or ag operators in Arizona or Texas.

title: Ratepayer Impact Statements for Data Centers
one_liner: An independent, quantified 'who pays' filing for every proposed data center, like an environmental impact statement but for your electric bill.
customer: Data center developers who need a credible neutral document to win zoning or PUC approval ($50-150k per project). County governments, state consumer advocates and ratepayer coalitions ($15-40k per docket) also buy it.
problem: 7 in 10 Americans oppose data centers in their community and New York imposed a hyperscale moratorium. Residential rates are up 7.3% and utilities requested a record $31B in hikes in 2025. Nobody can credibly say how much of a specific rate case or interconnection cost a given project causes, so each side hires ad hoc experts and the fight runs on vibes.
solution: An open, auditable cost-causation model built on FERC Form 1, EIA-861, large-load tariff filings, IRP capacity plans and PJM auction results. It outputs a 10-year per-household bill delta for a specific project under different tariff terms (minimum take, collateral, bring-your-own-capacity). Deliverables are a standardized Ratepayer Impact Statement and a witness-ready exhibit. A free state-by-state 'who pays' scorecard is the top of the funnel.
why_now: Affordability is a midterm issue and opposition is now bill-driven. Utilities are adopting large-load tariffs whose terms can be modeled. Capacity prices at the cap make cost shifts visible in dollars per MWh.
revenue_model: Per-project fee from developers, per-docket fee from advocates and counties, and an annual subscription for PUC staff. Independence comes from a published fee schedule and a methodology committed in advance, as with credit rating agencies.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders dismiss opposition as NIMBY, but it is really about bills, and bills are quantifiable. Whoever owns the accepted number owns the approval process. Both sides will pay for it, the way both sides accept an appraisal.
first_30_days: Publish a free 'Who Pays' report for three states using public filings. Email 10 state consumer advocate offices and 20 county planning departments. Offer a $12k pilot impact statement on one live docket. Approach two mid-size developers who are stuck in a zoning fight.

title: Flash-Heated Graphite Restoration From Anode Scrap
one_liner: Use flash Joule heating to restore spent and scrap anode graphite to usable grade in seconds, giving US anode makers a domestic, non-Chinese feedstock.
customer: US anode makers and cell manufacturers needing non-Chinese graphite (buyers), and cell-plant scrap managers (feedstock sellers).
problem: Graphite is a large share of black-mass weight, and hydromet recyclers typically treat it as waste. China dominates anode graphite, has tightened graphite export licensing, and the US has almost no domestic supply.
solution: A pulsed reactor (flash Joule heating, from academic work at Rice) purifies and re-graphitizes anode scrap at about 3000 K in seconds, using far less energy than conventional graphitization furnaces. The first product is a 100 kg/day pilot line producing qualification samples, with early sales into non-battery markets while battery-grade qualification proceeds.
why_now: Chinese graphite controls, US trade remedies, and rising domestic cell-plant scrap volumes all arrived in the last two years, and flash processing moved from lab papers to pilots.
revenue_model: Tolling or per-kg sale priced against imported anode-grade graphite, plus grants and offtake advance payments.
non_obvious_insight: Graphite is the one battery material that recycling plants throw away while the US has essentially no domestic supply.
first_30_days: License or build a bench flash reactor. Collect 500 kg of anode scrap from a cell-plant scrapper. Produce samples and send to 3 anode makers or national labs for coin-cell testing. File for DOE or DoD SBIR funding.

title: Cash Advances Against Steam Payouts
one_liner: A receivables-and-ad-float lender for live Steam games, underwritten from the studio's own Steamworks wishlist and sales data instead of the game's quality.
customer: Steam-live indie studios and micro-publishers with roughly $50k-$1M a year in net Steam revenue and 100+ reviews. They pay a flat fee of about 8-12% on each advance, repaid from Steam payouts.
problem: Valve pays about 30 days after month-end, so a launch-week spike reaches the bank up to two months later. In that gap the studio sees ads producing wishlists at a profit (say $1-2 per wishlist, with 15-25% converting to first-week sales) but has no cash to scale the spend, pay for a console port or fund localization. Indie Fund and new funds like Blue Ocean's $30M (2026) back development, not post-launch receivables. Banks treat games as hit-driven lotteries.
solution: A 'Payout Bridge'. The studio connects a read-only Steamworks financial and wishlist key. We forecast net receipts for the next 60-90 days from launch-day wishlists, demo conversion, regional mix and refund rate. We advance 30-50% of that forecast, or pay ad platforms and streamers directly as an 'ad float'. The studio points its Steam payout to a sweep account so repayment comes off the top. A free 'Steam funnel benchmark' dashboard built on the same keys is the top of the funnel and the data moat.
why_now: Steam gets roughly 20k releases a year, so marketing spend, not development, is now the main cost and the main cash-flow gap. Small funds are proving capital appetite for indies in 2026. Steam Machine (June 2026) and Steam Frame (Sept 2026) are widening the PC base. LLM tooling makes per-game underwriting cheap enough for $10-40k tickets.
revenue_model: A flat 8-12% fee on each advance, 60-120 day terms, with a fee premium for the ad-float product. Later: a subscription for the benchmark dashboard, and a securitized pool sold to a credit fund.
non_obvious_insight: A lender doesn't need the right tail that VCs obsess over. The first 30 days of Steam sales track launch-day wishlists within a fairly tight band, and Valve is a reliable payer. So credit risk is behavioural (the studio changing its bank details) and can be solved with a sweep account, not with taste in games. Underwrite the wishlist funnel and ignore game quality.
first_30_days: Ship the free Steamworks-key benchmark dashboard and seed it in Steam dev Discords, r/gamedev and the wishlist-marketing newsletters. Raise a $150-250k first-loss pool from angels or a small credit line. Manually underwrite 5-10 advances of $10-40k for studios that just launched or have a Next Fest spike. Get a fintech lawyer to structure it as a purchase of receivables.

title: Pattern-Less Foundry Network via Printed Sand Molds
one_liner: Print sand molds centrally and pour them at idle small foundries to deliver castings in about two weeks with no patterns.
customer: Pump, valve, ag-equipment and machinery OEMs and repair shops needing 5-500 castings. Small foundries are the supply side.
problem: Small-lot castings from Asia now face tariffs and freight up to 50% higher. Domestic foundries quote long lead times, largely because of pattern-making and minimum runs, and aging owners are retiring or closing. Castings are an invisible bottleneck under reshoring and under Section 232 derivative rates.
solution: A hub with binder-jet sand printing (or rented capacity at existing bureaus) prints mold and core packages from customer CAD plus solidification simulation. Ship them to 10-30 small foundries that pour iron, steel or aluminum. The network handles NDT, dimensional checks and certs, including melt origin. Start with one or two alloys and repair and replacement parts.
why_now: Printed sand has improved in cost and speed, tariffs and freight punish imported castings, foundries are consolidating, and simulation and AI gating design are cheap.
revenue_model: Per-casting pricing with 25-35% gross margin. $500-3k engineering fee per part. Foundries pay for mold volume routed to them.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck is patterns and scheduling, not melting. Many small foundries have idle furnace hours but no digital front door, and a printed mold is a universal interface. US-melt certification is a sales kicker, not the core.
first_30_days: Sign three foundries with idle capacity. Buy printed molds from an existing bureau. Take 10 orders for obsolete pump or gearbox housings at $1-3k each, using 3D scans of broken parts.

title: Zero-Retention Edge Enforcement for City Cameras
one_liner: Privacy-proof add-on analytics for existing plate readers and CCTV that keep only violation events and cryptographically delete everything else.
customer: Mid-size cities and towns in states that authorize automated enforcement (noise, illegal dumping, stop-arm, blocked bus lanes), starting with Connecticut, plus police departments under pressure over Flock-style data retention.
problem: Connecticut towns are bolting audio detectors onto existing plate readers for noise enforcement, while Ohio bills and public backlash attack camera surveillance. Cities want the revenue but fear becoming the next headline about bulk data retention.
solution: Edge box or firmware add-on that runs detection on-device and stores only the evidence clip for a confirmed violation. Everything else is deleted with signed deletion logs that auditors can verify. Sold as a rev-share enforcement program with a city-adoptable privacy ordinance template.
why_now: Connecticut's 2024 noise-camera law is live in West Haven, Wethersfield and East Hartford. Ohio bills show the Flock backlash is turning legislative. Cheap edge inference makes on-device analytics viable.
revenue_model: Per-citation or per-camera-month fee (for example 20-30% of net citation revenue, or $150-300 per camera per month), plus a one-time install fee.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders read the backlash as the end of sensor stacking. It is actually a moat for whoever makes data architecturally un-repurposable. Privacy becomes the procurement feature that survives a city council vote.
first_30_days: Pitch 5 Connecticut towns already running noise pilots to add a pilot with a retention-proof log. Build the demo on an off-the-shelf edge board with an existing LPR feed. Draft the ordinance template with a municipal attorney.

title: Metering Unmetered Wells From Orbit
one_liner: Estimate monthly pumping for every unmetered irrigation well by fusing radar subsidence, satellite crop water use and electricity data, and sell it to groundwater regulators.
customer: Groundwater sustainability agencies (about 140 in California), Texas groundwater conservation districts, Kansas management districts and Arizona active management areas, plus ag lenders, farmland funds and data-center developers relying on groundwater. Agencies pay annual fees.
problem: Most irrigation wells are unmetered, so regulators cannot enforce pumping limits or fees. Broad drought and Colorado River cuts push more pumping onto aquifers, and data centers in rule-of-capture states draw groundwater with little oversight.
solution: Fuse three signals: InSAR ground deformation (seasonal elastic movement tracks aquifer drawdown), ET-based irrigation demand minus effective precipitation, and pump electricity records from cooperating utilities. Calibrate against the wells that are metered and output pumping estimates with uncertainty per parcel and month. Deliver an evidence report agencies can use in fee and compliance programs.
why_now: The NASA-ISRO NISAR radar satellite launched in mid-2025 and its L-band data is open. ET datasets have matured. California's groundwater deadlines and the Texas audit push make measurement urgent.
revenue_model: $30-200k/yr per agency or basin, plus per-report fees to lenders and developers.
non_obvious_insight: Regulators do not need perfect meters, only defensible estimates calibrated against a sample of real ones, which is far cheaper than metering every well. The gap is that ET-only estimates cannot see storage change, and InSAR can.
first_30_days: Pick one critical-overdraft basin or Texas district with a metering plan. Reprocess two years of free Sentinel-1 InSAR, compare with the known meters, and publish a validation memo. Pitch three agencies on a 60-day paid pilot.

title: Independent Gauntlet for Police and Counter-Drone Buyers
angle: Pairing 2: Creator economy & media provenance x Government/public sector/defense/municipal services (creator-style trusted reviewer x dual-use municipal buyers)
one_liner: A buyer-funded, video-first test lab that flies and publishes open-protocol results on police first-responder drones and counter-drone detection, the way the Pentagon's public Gauntlets do for its own buyers, funded by agency subscriptions and never by vendors.
customer: Police, fire and emergency-management tech buyers at city and county agencies ($1,200-3,000 per agency-year for full data, vendor scorecards and RFP language), buyer consortia, and grant-funded counter-UAS programs (FEMA's $500M program, Dallas's $10M set-aside).
problem: Local buyers cannot audit vendors: state and local tech contracts average 7 years, only 5.3% of AI-relevant provisions address transparency, and GenAI-written RFPs make every proposal look perfect. Vendor claims are unreliable: only 24% of drones reached 10 km in the Pentagon's Gauntlet 1, Cape Canaveral's radars miss quadcopters, and 700+ drones were seized around one World Cup stadium. Trade media and cooperative marketplaces are vendor-funded, so independent performance data does not exist.
solution: Quarterly standardized tests covering range, wind, latency, false alarms against birds and RF clutter, and detection of cooperative test drones only (no jamming). Runs are recorded with signed telemetry and raw video so results cannot be disputed or edited, and protocols are open. Drone creators co-host as pilots and distribute the long-form video, while agencies pay for data, scorecards, sample RFP language and an ask-us desk. Vendors may buy re-tests only after results are public.
why_now: The Pentagon's public Gauntlets (Gauntlet 2 in Sept 2026: 23 platforms, 19 companies, 1,858 sorties) normalized head-to-head public testing. Counter-drone money is flowing to cities, sponsored and AI-written content swamps review media, and local surveillance-tech purchases now face public scrutiny.
revenue_model: Agency subscriptions, custom pre-procurement tests paid from grants, and paid training. No vendor sponsorship, which is the trust asset.
non_obvious_insight: DoD's Gauntlet works because the buyer controls the test. Local agencies have the same need but no lab budget, and the creator-media model (audience-funded, no sponsors) is exactly the structure that makes an independent lab self-sustaining. Vendor-funded trade media and vendor-listing marketplaces are structurally unable to be the referee.
first_30_days: Buy five sub-$5K first-responder-class drones and run one head-to-head on range, wind and latency, then publish it. Email 200 police tech sergeants and drone-as-first-responder coordinators and sign 10 agency subscriptions at $1,200. File public-records requests for existing agency test data to seed the second episode.

title: Hyperspectral Target Packs for Natural Hydrogen Explorers
one_liner: Use newly open hyperspectral satellite data to rank licence blocks for natural hydrogen, then sell the evidence pack that helps cash-poor explorers raise money and keep their licences.
customer: Junior explorers and startups holding or applying for natural-hydrogen licences (ASX/TSXV juniors, private startups, landmen leasing in the US Midcontinent, Spain, France, South Australia and the Philippines), plus government surveys running tenders.
problem: Licences and leases are being granted essentially blind in a land rush. Drilling costs millions, and the only surface clues are ultramafic and iron-rich rock, vegetation anomalies and circular depressions. Small explorers cannot afford a full geophysics programme yet need credible evidence for investors and regulators.
solution: A multi-sensor prospectivity pack: hyperspectral mineral mapping (EMIT, Planet Tanager open data, Pixxel tasking) for serpentinized ultramafic rocks and iron-oxide and clay alteration; multi-year vegetation-stress anomalies; Sentinel-2 and SAR detection of circular depressions; then public gravity/magnetics and geology. Output is a ranked block list and a 20-page evidence deck, with an optional partner ground-truth soil-gas hydrogen survey.
why_now: Koloma has raised about $400M and won the first competitive natural-hydrogen bid round in the Philippines (three contracts, over 4,000 km2). A USGS map, DOE grants, EU funding (Mantle 8) and Australian co-funding are all live. Open hyperspectral archives (EMIT, Tanager) and cheap commercial tasking (Pixxel Firefly, about $8/km2 quoted) did not exist three years ago.
revenue_model: $10k to $40k per licence-block pack. $3k to $8k a month monitoring retainer. For cash-poor juniors, part-payment via a small royalty or option in place of cash.
non_obvious_insight: In a gold rush, the scarce product is a credible map that makes the pitch deck and licence renewal defensible, and hyperspectral is unusually good at the specific rock chemistry of serpentinization. You sell ranking plus a ground-truth feedback loop, not certainty, and each drill or soil-gas result improves the model in a way competitors cannot copy.
first_30_days: Back-test on known hydrogen occurrences and known fairy-circle areas to measure hit rate. Publish a free prospectivity map of one region (Kansas/Nebraska Midcontinent Rift or South Australia) to attract leads. Sell three packs to ASX or TSXV juniors at $10k to $15k.

title: Cash-Flow Lifeline for K-12 Service Vendors
one_liner: Same-week invoice funding for small vendors who serve schools (after-school, tutoring, therapy, van companies), priced using each district's known payment calendar, with a service-continuity guarantee for principals.
customer: Small K-12 vendors paying a financing fee: after-school providers, contract speech, occupational and counseling practices, tutoring companies, small van and transportation contractors, and arts and PE providers. Principals are the sponsor and the free channel.
problem: Districts pay invoices 60 to 120 days late, and federal-grant reimbursements (21st Century, Title programs) lag further. Small vendors run out of cash and vanish in October, mid-year, leaving kids without services. Principals cannot legally pay faster and get blamed when the therapist stops coming. Generic factoring companies price district risk like a private customer or refuse it.
solution: Fund invoices within 48 hours at 90 percent advance. Verification is a text or QR 'services delivered' confirmation from the principal, which is the step district accounts payable needs anyway. Price risk using each district's board-approval calendar, warrant runs and reimbursement cycles, which we assemble from public board minutes. Add a continuity guarantee: if a funded vendor fails, a pre-vetted bench vendor steps in. Districts get a simple notice-of-assignment form to sign.
why_now: The July 2025 withholding of roughly $6.8B in federal education funds, released weeks later, showed how fragile the timing is. Post-ESSER budgets are tight, and small-business credit is harder for vendors with slow government customers. LLMs can now read board packets, purchase orders and approval calendars at scale to predict pay dates.
revenue_model: Fee of about 1.5 to 3 percent per invoice per 30 days advanced, plus a vendor subscription ($99 per month) for the delivery-confirmation and invoicing workflow.
non_obvious_insight: District default risk is near zero. The risk is timing, and timing is predictable if you know how boards and warrant runs work. The principal's confirmation, not the bank, is the bottleneck, so whoever owns that step owns the data. Investors dismiss K-12 as slow and poor, but the payer is a taxing authority, which is the safest receivable there is.
first_30_days: Recruit 10 small vendors from principals' and coordinators' contact lists, starting with after-school and therapy contractors that have already had payment problems. Raise $150k to $300k of angel or warehouse capital and fund the first invoices at a flat fee. Build the district payment calendars in a spreadsheet from public minutes, which becomes the pricing model and the data moat.

title: Mahjong Leagues for Senior Living Communities
one_liner: A turnkey mahjong program (kits, instructors, scoring app, inter-community leagues) sold to senior-living activity directors.
customer: Activity directors at independent and assisted living communities (roughly 30k in the US), 55+ HOAs, and library systems.
problem: Mahjong is booming: CNN (19 Sept 2026) covers the explosion, Yelp searches for mahjong clubs rose about 4,467% in 2025, and the National Mah Jongg League reports 350k+ members. Coverage frames it as a Gen Z and millennial aesthetic trend. Meanwhile senior-living calendars need social, cognitive, low-injury weekly activities, and American mahjong is hard to learn and hard to staff with teachers.
solution: A subscription with a 4-table starter kit, certified instructor visits (in person or video), monthly inter-community league nights with a shared leaderboard and trophy, a coordinator app, and staff training so the community can run it alone.
why_now: The mainstream boom is producing demand and a supply of instructors from the new club scene. Pickleball injuries make low-impact alternatives attractive for the same age group.
revenue_model: $300-600/month per community, $250 kits, per-visit instructor fees, and tile-maker sponsorships.
non_obvious_insight: Tile brands and influencers chase young buyers with $200 designer sets. The recurring money sits with older players who play weekly and with institutions that have a budget line called 'activities'. Inter-facility leagues create retention and sales compounding, because a community that joins forces its rivals to join.
first_30_days: Approach 20 senior communities in one metro via activity-director networks. Run free two-week pilots staffed by 2 volunteer instructors recruited from local clubs. Convert 5 into $300/month accounts and stage the first inter-community match.

title: Bonded Claims: Bug Bounties for Product Labels
one_liner: Brands post a forfeitable bond behind a testable label claim, and anyone can buy the product, get it lab-tested and collect the bond if the claim is false.
customer: Mid-size DTC supplement, protein, baby-food and pet-food brands whose 'third-party tested' or 'heavy-metal free' claims are doubted, plus retail and marketplace buyers who want evidence and insurers.
problem: Label claims cannot be checked on the shelf. Certifications are one-time and paid for by the certified. Heavy-metal and potency class actions are routine, and gray-market peptide vendors forge certificates of analysis (FDA warning letters to seven online sellers, Mar 2026). Honest brands cannot distinguish themselves.
solution: A claim registry. The brand states a specific, machine-checkable claim (for example lead below X per serving, or label potency within 10%), posts a $10-50k bond in escrow and accepts a protocol: retail-purchased units, an accredited lab, and blinded replicates. Challengers pay for tests or use subsidised credits, and a neutral panel confirms chain of custody. A failed claim pays the challenger and forfeits the bond and badge. A claim that survives N challenges earns a 'survived challenge' tier that retail buyers can query by API.
why_now: Finnrick has now published 10,000+ independent peptide tests, proving that crowds will fund lab tests of vendors. Heavy-metal exposés and lawsuits keep recurring. Stablecoin and card-hold escrow make small bonds cheap to run. Retailers want a liability shield for clean-label shelves.
revenue_model: $2-5k annual listing fee, a 1-3% bond-management fee, challenge-processing fees, and retailer API licences.
non_obvious_insight: Bug bounties worked in software because they turn hostile sceptics into paid auditors. Physical-goods certification does the opposite and pays friendly auditors. A bond makes the brand fund the scepticism, and only honest brands can afford to post one, which gives the badge a real price premium.
first_30_days: Approach 10 clean-label brands that already publish certificates of analysis (creatine, collagen, omega-3, kids' vitamins) and pitch it as cheaper than class-action defence. Sign one ISO 17025 lab for a fixed test panel. Run a public 'challenge week' with a supplement community, using a standard escrow account.

title: Paid Exit Capture: Layoffs Become Agent Evals
one_liner: Pay departing employees a completion bonus to turn their tacit exception-handling know-how into the eval sets and edge-case playbooks the employer's AI agents need, before that knowledge walks out.
customer: Head of AI, COO or CHRO at 1,000-20,000-person companies running AI-justified headcount cuts in ops-heavy functions (claims, support, finance ops, procurement), plus PE operating partners doing portfolio-wide cuts.
problem: Companies cut the people who know the long tail, then find their agents fail on it. Reversals are now reported (Klarna rehiring humans in 2025, Commonwealth Bank of Australia reversing 45 cuts, CNBC's Jul 2026 'regret' headline). Exit interviews are HR theatre, and angry leavers have no reason to document anything.
solution: A 2-3 week 'capture sprint' inside the notice or severance window. A consented, paid interview agent plus a domain reviewer walks each person through their 50 hardest cases. Output is a graded eval set (inputs, gold decisions, rubrics, 'when I'd escalate') and a playbook the employer owns. Workers get a bonus scaled to eval quality (measured by held-out agent accuracy), a signed contribution credential and optionally a recall or contract-rights clause.
why_now: AI was the top-cited layoff reason in Challenger data for five straight months through Jul 2026, and enterprise agent rollouts are now bottlenecked by evals and edge cases rather than by models. Reversal stories are giving CFOs a fresh fear. Interview agents are cheap enough to run the sprints at scale.
revenue_model: $15-40k fixed fee per role-cluster capture sprint (roughly $1.5-4k per captured employee after bonuses), plus an annual eval-refresh retainer once the agent is live.
non_obvious_insight: To the employer a laid-off worker is a depreciating liability, but for the agent rollout they are the only source of ground truth on the long tail. You can only get it by paying, and paying on eval quality fixes the incentive. The data is worth far more than the severance delta.
first_30_days: Use public WARN filings to list 40 companies mid-layoff and pitch 15 HR/AI leads a free 5-person pilot at cost. Have an employment lawyer draft the consent, IP-assignment and NDA carve-out template. Deliver one eval set and show before/after agent accuracy as the case study.

title: GLP-1 Palate Panel for Food R&D
one_liner: A managed panel of GLP-1 users and their households that food and restaurant companies rent to test products, portions and health claims.
customer: R&D and insights teams at mid-size CPG (protein, snacks, frozen), restaurant chain menu teams, foodservice for hospitals and senior living, and supplement brands that need claim substantiation ($25-150k per study).
problem: 73% of GLP-1 users report taste changes and 70% lose joy in eating, so 'just add protein' fails. About 70% change what the household eats, and non-users adopt 30-50% of the changes, so the affected base is ~50% larger than the user count. Food companies are reformulating and launching 'GLP-1 friendly' labels on general-population panels and conflicting forecasts.
solution: Recruit and maintain a segmented panel (drug, dose, weeks on therapy, aversion profile, household makeup). Run sensory, portion and format tests plus home-use tests and 8-12 week muscle and satiety claim studies. Deliver 'aversion maps' (which textures and smells trigger nausea at which dose) and household spillover models.
why_now: Households with a GLP-1 user doubled from ~11% to 22% in under 3 years. Pills launched in 2026 broaden the base. CPG is mid-reformulation, and FTC claim scrutiny makes 'evidence-backed' labels valuable. Purchase-panel incumbents see what is bought, not why.
revenue_model: $25-150k per study, plus $40-100k/year data subscription for 'aversion map' updates.
non_obvious_insight: The 'GLP-1 consumer' is 5-6 sensory segments that shift with dose and week on therapy, not one persona. Forecasting from sales data cannot separate them, but a panel can. The picks-and-shovels of a reformulation wave are the testers, not the brands.
first_30_days: Recruit 300 panelists from subreddits and Facebook groups with a $25 incentive, verified by photo of the pharmacy label. Publish a free 'taste change' survey report for press. Cold-email 30 CPG insights leads and land a first paid pilot of about $25k.

title: Gig Income Shock Cover From Pooled Data
one_liner: Insure the algorithm: pay drivers when they are deactivated or when regional platform earnings collapse, using pooled earnings data to defeat moral hazard.
customer: Rideshare and delivery drivers through driver co-ops, forums and earnings-tracking apps, and credit unions that finance drivers' cars.
problem: A deactivation or algorithmic pay cut can remove 30-100% of a driver's income overnight with no unemployment insurance, while record auto delinquencies (brief) mean many drivers carry stressed car loans. Individual income insurance has historically failed on moral hazard and adverse selection.
solution: A membership cover paying 2-4 weeks of trailing average earnings on (a) a verified platform deactivation, or (b) a regional earnings-per-hour index falling more than 25% against baseline, computed from pooled, driver-consented earnings data. Structure it through a fronting carrier or discretionary mutual, and offer credit unions a car-payment protection version.
why_now: Record auto delinquencies, growing algorithmic management of pay, driver data cooperatives and earnings-tracking apps that already pool consented data, and instant payout rails.
revenue_model: $10-$20 per month premium, credit-union-paid group premium bundled with car loans, and anonymized index data licensing.
non_obvious_insight: Moral hazard is the classic reason income insurance fails, but a platform-controlled event (deactivation) and a pooled regional index are not something the worker can game. The data cooperatives already exist and are the missing underwriting input.
first_30_days: Partner with one driver co-op or large forum for a 300-member paid pilot with a capped reserve. Collect earnings-data consents, back-test the index triggers on historical data, and have a fronting partner review the structure.
